**Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on Surah 29, verse 1:**

﴿Alif Lam Mim﴾. It has been mentioned in al-Baqara.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 29, verse 2:

﴿Do people think that they will be left [to say], "We believe," and they will not be tested?﴾ It was revealed concerning a group of believers who were in Mecca and were oppressed, among them ʿAmmar ibn Yasir and others. The disbelievers of Quraysh would harm them and torture them for [embracing] Islam, so their hearts were constricted by this. Then God comforted them with this verse, admonished them, and informed them that this [affliction] is a trial, so that they might prepare themselves to be patient under harm and steadfast in faith. God the Exalted thus informed them that this is His way with His servants: He empowers the disbelievers over the believers in order to purify them through it, and to make manifest the truthful in his faith from the liar. Its wording is nonetheless general, so its ruling applies universally to everyone who is struck by a trial, whether a calamity or a harm to the self, wealth, or otherwise. The meaning of ﴿ḥasiba﴾ is "thought" (ẓanna), and ﴿an yuträkū﴾ is its object; the hamza is for denial (al-inkār). ﴿wa-hum lā yuftanūn﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in yutrakū; its estimated sense is "not being tested." And ﴿an yaqūlū﴾ is a causal clause in the position of the object of purpose (mafʿūl min ajlih).

﴿So Allah will surely make known those who are truthful﴾. That is, He will make manifest their truthfulness as an observed reality in existence, although His knowledge of it was already eternal. The "truthfulness" and "falsehood" in the verse mean the soundness of faith and its steadfastness, or the opposite of that.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 29, verse 4:

﴿Or do those who commit evil deeds think that they can outrun Us?﴾ "Am" (or) is an equivalent (mu'adilah) to His saying: ﴿Do people think...﴾ The intended meaning of ﴿those who commit evil deeds﴾ is the disbelievers who persecute the believers; yet the wording, in addition to this, is general, covering every disbeliever or disobedient person. The meaning of "yasbiquna" (outrun us) is: they escape from Our punishment and render Us powerless. So the sense of the statement is the negation of their outrunning (Us). Just as the meaning of the verse before it is the negation of leaving the believers without being tested.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 29, verse 5:

﴿Whoever hopes for the meeting with Allah﴾ [and so on, the verse]: It is a consolation to the believers and a promise of good for them in the Hereafter. Here "hope" (al-raja') retains its original meaning. It has also been said that it means "fear." ﴿The term of Allah﴾ is death. The meaning of the verse is: whoever hopes for the reward of Allah, let him be patient in this world, persevering in striving in obedience to Allah, until he meets Allah, who will then recompense him, for the meeting with Allah is near in coming, and everything that is coming is near.

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿And whoever strives, only strives for himself﴾

"Its benefit: the benefit of his striving belongs only to himself, for God is not benefited by the obedience of His servants. Jihad here may mean fighting (qital), or the striving against the self (jihad al-nafs)."

Ḥusnan (حُسْناً) is in the accusative, governed by a hidden verb whose sense is: "And We enjoined upon man that he treat his parents kindly (ḥasanan)." Alternatively, it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) derived from the meaning of "We enjoined" (waṣṣaynā), i.e., "an excellent injunction."

﴿And if they strive with you to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, do not obey them.﴾ The verse was revealed concerning Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, who, when he embraced Islam, his mother swore that she would not shade herself with any shade until he disbelieved. It was also said that it was revealed concerning others to whom a similar thing happened. So God commanded them to remain steadfast in Islam and not to obey their parents when they command them to disbelieve. He expressed the parents' command as "striving" (jihād) as an intensification.

**[Qur'an 29:10]** "And among the people is one who says, 'We believe in Allah,'"

It was revealed concerning a people who were believers in their tongues only. When the disbelievers tortured them, they turned back from faith. Then when Allah gave victory to the believers, they said, "We were with you." So the meaning of "harmed for the sake of Allah" is that he is harmed because of his faith in Allah. "The trial of people" means their torment. It is also said that it was revealed concerning 'Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'ah, the maternal half-brother of Abu Jahl.

Follow Our way (ittabi'u sabilana): that is, the disbelievers said to the believers: "Disbelieve as we have disbelieved, and we will bear for you the sin and punishment, if there is any." It is related that the one who uttered this statement was al-Walid ibn al-Mughira; al-Mahdawi transmitted this.

As for their saying ﴿And let us bear your sins﴾ (wa-li-nahmil khataya-kum): it is the consequence of their saying "Follow Our way." They expressed it in the form of a command for emphasis. Since the meaning of the statement is a report, its falsehood was made clear, so God informed them that they are liars: that is, they will not bear the burdens of those people, rather they will bear their own burdens and the burdens of their followers among the disbelievers.

**"So he remained among them a thousand years less fifty years."** The apparent meaning is that he remained this period after his being sent (as a prophet). It is also possible that this is counted from the beginning of his birth. It is narrated that he was sent when he was forty years old, and that he lived after the Flood three hundred and fifty years. If it is asked: why did He say "a thousand years," and then say "less fifty years"? The wording differs while the meaning is the same? The answer is that this is to avoid repeating the word "sanah" (year), since repetition is disliked, except when it is intended for magnification or to emphasize the enormity.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 29, verse 15:

﴿And We made it a sign﴾ It is possible that the pronoun refers to the ship, or to the deliverance, or to the whole story in its entirety.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 29, verse 17:

﴿And you fashion a lie﴾ — it is from creation (al-khalq), and he means by it the carving of idols; he called it "creation" in a figurative sense (tajawwuz). It was also said that it is from fabricating lies (ikhtilaq al-kadhib). ﴿They do not possess for you any provision﴾ — the verse is an argument for the Oneness (al-wahdaniyyah) of God and the negation of partners. If it is asked: why did He make "provision" indefinite (nakirah) at first, then make it definite in His words: ﴿so seek provision from God﴾? The answer: He made it indefinite in His words ﴿they do not possess for you any provision﴾ for the purpose of generality in negation, since an indefinite noun in the context of negation implies generality. Then He made it definite after that, for the purpose of generality in seeking provision, all of it, from God, because an indefinite noun in the context of affirmation does not imply generality except with definiteness. It is as if He said: seek all the provision from God.

"And if you deny" — the verse. It may be part of Abraham's speech, or part of the speech of God Most High. It may also be meant as a warning and threat to the disbelievers, or it may be meant as consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding his people's denial of him, by taking as a model the other prophets whose peoples denied them.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 29, verses 19–21:

﴿Have they not seen how Allah originates creation?﴾ It is said: "badaa Allahu al-khalq" and "abda'ahu" with one meaning (bada'a and ab'da'a both mean to originate). Both forms have come in this surah. The meaning: Have not the disbelievers seen that Allah created creation, so that they may infer from the first creation the return (i'adah) at the gathering (al-hashr)? As for His saying: ﴿then He repeats it﴾, it is not coordinated (ma'tuf) with "yubdi'" (originates), because the meaning of the two differs: seeing the origination is by direct observation, whereas the repetition is known through reflection (nazar) and inference (istidlal). Rather, it is coordinated with the whole clause. It has been said that it refers to the regrowth (i'adah) and the initiation of plants, and on this reading ﴿then He repeats it﴾ would be coordinated with "yubdi'" because the meaning is the same. The first view is better and more fitting to the aims of the discourse. ﴿Indeed that, for Allah, is easy﴾, meaning the repetition of creation, which is their gathering. Then He commanded them to travel in the earth so that they may see the creatures of Allah and infer from them His power to gather them. For this reason He concluded with His saying: ﴿Indeed Allah is over all things competent﴾. ﴿And to Him you will be turned back﴾, i.e., you will be returned.

Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 29, verse 23:

﴿Those have despaired of My mercy﴾. It is possible that their despair refers to the Hereafter, or that it describes their state in this world, since the disbeliever despairs of Allah's mercy while the believer is hopeful and fearful. This statement, from His words ﴿Do they not see...﴾ up to here, may be addressed to Muhammad (ﷺ) as an interjection between the story of Ibrahim, or it may be addressed to Ibrahim, and after that He mentions the answer of his people to him.

﴿مَّوَدَّةَ بَيْنِكُمْ﴾ The word مودة (mawaddah, "affection") is in the accusative either as an object of purpose (مفعول من أجله, maf'ul min ajlihi) or as the second object of اتخذتم (ittakhadhtum, "you have taken"). It may also be in the nominative, as the predicate of an implied subject (خبر ابتداء مضمر, khabar ibtida' mudmar) or as the predicate of إن (inna). In that case ما (ma) is a relative pronoun (موصولة, mawsulah). The word بينكم (baynakum, "between you") is in the accusative as an adverb of place (على الظرفية, 'ala al-zarfiyyah), and it may be in the genitive by being construed as a genitive construct (بالإضافة, bi'l-idafah).

Translation:

﴿So Lut believed in him﴾. The verb "āmana" (believed) here implies "infaqada" (submitted to, yielded to), and for that reason it takes the preposition "lām" (to/for). ﴿And he said, "Indeed I am emigrating to my Lord"﴾. The one who said this is Ibrahim, and it was said that it was Lut. The two of them emigrated from their lands, from the land of Babylon, to al-Sham (Greater Syria).

﴿And We placed in his descendants prophethood and the Book﴾. Most of the prophets were from the descendants of Ibrahim (Abraham), and upon his descendants God sent down the Tawrat, the Injil, the Zabur, and the Furqan.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 29, verse 29:

﴿And you cut off the road﴾. It is said that he meant highway robbery for plunder and killing; and it is said that he meant cutting off the path of procreation by abandoning women and approaching men. ﴿And you commit evil in your assemblies﴾. The nadi (assembly) is the gathering place where people come together, and the munkar (evil) is their act with men. It is also said that it refers to their harming of people.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 29, verse 31–34:

﴿And when Our messengers came to Abraham with the good news﴾ The messengers here are the angels, and the good news is the announcement to Abraham of a son, as in His saying: ﴿So We gave him the good news of a forbearing boy﴾ [al-Saffat: 101]. Or it is the good news of the victory of our master Lot, and the first is more apparent. ﴿The people of this town﴾ meaning the town of our master Lot. ﴿He said, "Indeed, Lot is there"﴾ This is not an informing that he is there; rather, he intended the deliverance of our master Lot from the punishment that would befall the people of the town, and his innocence of the wrongdoing with which they had described him. It is as if he said: How will you destroy the people of the town while Lot is in it, and how will you say they are wrongdoers while Lot is among them? ﴿Among those who remain behind﴾ has already been mentioned. Likewise ﴿He was distressed on their account﴾ and ﴿a punishment from the sky﴾, meaning a punishment.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on surah 29, verses 36–37:

﴿And hope for the Last Day﴾. It is said: "hope" here means "fear." It is also said: it retains its original meaning. ﴿And do not commit corruption on the earth﴾, meaning: they used to cheat in the measure and the scale. ﴿The earthquake﴾ is the (loud) cry.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 29, verses 38–40:

﴿And it has become clear to you from their dwellings﴾: that is, the traces of their dwellings remain, indicating what befell them. ﴿And they were discerning﴾ (mustabsirin). It is said: its meaning is that they had insight into their disbelief and were pleased with it. It is also said: they had insight into faith, but they disbelieved out of obstinacy. And it is said: the meaning of "mustabsirin" is that they were intelligent and able to reflect and draw inferences, but they did not do so. ﴿And they were not ones who could escape﴾: that is, they could not elude Us. ﴿So of them is one upon whom We sent a hasib (a violent storm of stones)﴾. Al-hasib means stones, and al-hasib also means a violent wind. In my view it may be that He intended both meanings, because the people of Prophet Lut were destroyed by stones, and 'Ad were destroyed by wind. If we take the word in only one meaning, the mention of the other is lost. Many scholars have permitted the use of a single word in two meanings, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet﴾ [al-Ahzab: 56]. This is strengthened here, because the purpose is to mention the all-inclusive seizure of the categories of disbelievers. ﴿And of them is one who was seized by the Blast﴾, meaning Thamud and Madyan. ﴿And of them is one whom We caused the earth to swallow﴾, meaning Qarun. ﴿And of them is one whom We drowned﴾, meaning the people of Nuh and Fir'awn and his people.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 29, verse 41:

﴿The parable of those who take protectors other than Allah is like the spider, which takes a house; and indeed, the weakest of houses is the spider's house, if only they knew.﴾

Allah likened the disbelievers in their worship of idols to the spider in its building of a weak house. What the spider relies on in its house is nothing, so likewise what the disbelievers rely on of their gods is nothing, because they neither benefit nor harm. ﴿The weakest of houses﴾ means the most feeble of them. ﴿If only they knew﴾ means: if only they knew that this is their parable.

Indeed, Allah knows what they call upon besides Him of anything. "Ma" here is a relative pronoun meaning "that which," functioning as the object of the verb preceding it. It is also said that "ma" is a negation particle, and the verb is suspended from operating on what follows it. According to this reading, the meaning is: you do not call upon anything besides Allah that has any significance, so it is not fitting to call it "a thing."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 29, verse 44:

﴿Bi-l-ḥaqq﴾ That is, "with truth," meaning with what is required (wājib), not in a manner of idleness and play.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 29, verse 45:

﴿Indeed, the prayer forbids immorality and wrongdoing﴾ If the one praying is humbly submissive (khashi') in his prayer, mindful of the greatness of the One before whom he stands, this leads him to repent of immorality and wrongdoing; so it is as if the prayer is what forbids them. ﴿And the remembrance of Allah is greater﴾ It has been said that there are three meanings to this. The first: the meaning is that the prayer is greater than other acts of obedience, and it is named "the remembrance of Allah" because the remembrance of Allah is the greatest thing in it. By this he points to the reason for its forbidding immorality and wrongdoing, because the remembrance of Allah within it is what forbids immorality and wrongdoing. The second: the remembrance of Allah at all times is greater in forbidding immorality and wrongdoing than the prayer, because the prayer occurs at some times and not others. The third: the remembrance of Allah is greater in reward than the prayer and than all other acts of obedience, as is reported in the hadith: "Shall I not inform you of the best of your deeds?" They said: "Yes." He said: "The remembrance of Allah."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 29, verse 46:

﴿And do not argue with the People of the Book except in a way that is best﴾ That is, do not argue with the disbelievers among the People of the Book when you differ with them regarding religion, except in the way that is best, not by striking or fighting. This was before jihad was prescribed, and then it was abrogated (naskh) by the sword. The meaning of ﴿except those who have wronged﴾ is: those who wronged you and openly harmed your Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ). It has also been said that the meaning of the verse is: do not argue with those among the People of the Book who have embraced Islam concerning the reports they related to you, except in the way that is best. And the meaning of "except those who have wronged," according to this view, is those among them who remained upon their disbelief. The first meaning is more apparent. ﴿And say, "We believe"﴾ This and what follows implies a kind of agreement and peaceful coexistence, and it has been abrogated by the sword. It also implies turning away from conversing with them. And in a hadith: "Do not believe the People of the Book, nor disbelieve them, and say: We believe in what has been sent down to us and sent down to you. If what they say is false, you have not believed them; and if it is true, you have not disbelieved them."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 29, verse 47:

﴿And thus We have sent down to you the Book﴾. That is, just as We sent down the Book upon those before you, We have sent it down upon you. ﴿So those to whom We have given the Book﴾: he means ʿAbdullah ibn Salam and those like him, from among the Jews and Christians who embraced Islam. ﴿And among these there are some who believe in it﴾. He intends by "those to whom the Book was given" the people of the Torah and the Gospel, and by his words ﴿and among these there are some who believe in it﴾ the disbelievers of Quraysh. It has also been said: by "those to whom the Book was given" he means the earlier people of the Torah and the Gospel, and by "these" he means those among them who were contemporaries of Muhammad (ﷺ), such as ʿAbdullah ibn Salam.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 29, verse 48:

﴿Nor did you recite any scripture before it, nor did you write one with your right hand.﴾ This is an argument that the Qur'an is from Allah, because the Prophet (ﷺ) could neither read nor write, and yet he brought the Qur'an. If it is asked: what is the purpose of his words "with your right hand"? The answer is that it is an emphasis on the statement and a depiction of the intended meaning. ﴿Otherwise, those who spread falsehood would have had cause for doubt.﴾ That is, if you had been able to read or write, doubt would have crept in among the disbelievers, and they would have said: "Perhaps he learned this Book or read it." It has also been said that the basis of the argument is that the People of the Book used to find in their scriptures that the Prophet (ﷺ) was an unlettered man who could neither read nor write. When Allah made him so, the proof was established against them. Had he been able to read or write, he would have contradicted the description by which Allah had described him among them. The correct position is that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) never read or wrote at all. Al-Bajji and others said that he did write, based on the apparent wording of the hadith of al-Hudaybiyya, but this view is weak.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 29, verse 49:

﴿Rather, it is clear signs﴾. The pronoun refers to the Qur'an, and the shift marked by "bal" (rather, a particle of reversal) is away from an omitted statement, whose sense is: the matter is not as the wrongdoers and the falsehood-followers supposed.

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down to you the Book﴾ — the meaning: how do they ask for a sign when the Qur'an is the greatest of signs and the clearest in indicating the truth of prophethood? Why not let it suffice them instead of seeking other signs? ﴿Say: "Sufficient is God as a witness between me and you"﴾. Its meaning has been mentioned in Surat al-Ra'd [43] and in al-An'am.

Why not let it suffice them instead of seeking other signs? ﴿Say: "Sufficient is God as a witness between me and you"﴾. Its meaning has been mentioned in Surat al-Ra'd [43] and in al-An'am.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 29, verses 53–54:

﴿They ask you to hasten the punishment﴾. The pronoun refers to the disbelievers, meaning their saying: ﴿Bring upon us what you threaten us with﴾ [al-A'raf: 77], and their saying: ﴿Rain down upon us stones from the sky﴾ [al-Anfal: 32], and the like. ﴿Had it not been for a term appointed﴾, meaning: had it not been that God had decreed for their punishment a specified term, it would have come upon them when they asked for it. ﴿And it will surely come upon them suddenly while they are unaware﴾. It may mean the killing that befell them on the day of Badr, or the hunger that befell them through the successive years of drought, or it may mean the punishment of the Hereafter, and this is more evident given His saying: ﴿And indeed, Hell is encompassing the disbelievers﴾.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 29, verses 53–54:

﴿They ask you to hasten the punishment﴾. The pronoun refers to the disbelievers, meaning their saying: ﴿Bring upon us what you threaten us with﴾ [al-A'raf: 77], and their saying: ﴿Rain down upon us stones from the sky﴾ [al-Anfal: 32], and the like. ﴿Had it not been for a term appointed﴾, meaning: had it not been that God had decreed for their punishment a specified term, it would have come upon them when they asked for it. ﴿And it will surely come upon them suddenly while they are unaware﴾. It may mean the killing that befell them on the day of Badr, or the hunger that befell them through the successive years of drought, or it may mean the punishment of the Hereafter, and this is more evident given His saying: ﴿And indeed, Hell is encompassing the disbelievers﴾.
﴿The day the punishment will envelop them﴾ means it will surround them. The element governing the adverbial phrase (al-zarf) is either omitted or is the one that encompasses them.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 29, verse 56:

﴿Indeed, My earth is vast﴾ — an exhortation to emigrate from Mecca, since the believers were suffering the harm of the disbelievers there, and an encouragement to seek another land of God. Thereupon they emigrated to the land of Abyssinia (al-Habasha), and then to Medina.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 29, verse 58:

﴿Surely We shall lodge them﴾ means: We shall settle them (ننزلنهم). Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read it as nuthwiyannahum (نثوينهم), with the letter thā' (ث) having three dots, from al-thawā, which means dwelling and staying in a place.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 29, verse 60–61:

﴿And how many a creature there is that does not carry its provision; Allah provides for it and for you.﴾ That is: how many a weak creature there is that is unable to carry its provision, yet Allah provides for it despite its weakness. The purpose of the verse is to strengthen the hearts of the believers when they fear poverty and hunger in migrating to the lands of people; that is, just as Allah provides for weak animals, so He will provide for you if you migrate from your land. ﴿And if you asked them﴾ (in both places): establishing proof against them. ﴿the All-Knowing﴾: that is, how they are turned away from the truth.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 29, verse 60–61:

﴿And how many a creature there is that does not carry its provision; Allah provides for it and for you.﴾ That is: how many a weak creature there is that is unable to carry its provision, yet Allah provides for it despite its weakness. The purpose of the verse is to strengthen the hearts of the believers when they fear poverty and hunger in migrating to the lands of people; that is, just as Allah provides for weak animals, so He will provide for you if you migrate from your land. ﴿And if you asked them﴾ (in both places): establishing proof against them. ﴿the All-Knowing﴾: that is, how they are turned away from the truth.

"Say: 'Praise be to Allah.'" (Praise of Allah for the manifestation of the proof.) The meaning is that they are obliged to praise Allah, since they acknowledged that He created the heavens and the earth. "But most of them do not understand." (This is a turning away from a omitted statement, whose implied meaning is: it is incumbent upon them to worship Allah, since they acknowledged it, but they do not understand.)

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 29, verse 64:

﴿Truly, this is the [true] life﴾ — i.e., the everlasting life in which there is no death. The word al-hayawan (ḥayawān, "life/living") is a verbal noun (maṣdar) like al-hayah (ḥayāh, "life").

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 29, verse 65:

﴿So when they board the ship﴾ and so on (the verse): It is a proof established against them by their supplication at times of hardship, and then they associate others with Him in a state of ease.

Translation:

﴿That they may deny⁠﴾ is a command in the form of a threat, or in the form of abandonment and leaving [them to themselves], just as you say to someone whose advice you give but who does not accept it: "Do what you wish."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 29, verse 67:

﴿Have they not seen that We made a secure sanctuary (ḥaram āmin)﴾ The pronoun refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh. The secure sanctuary is Makkah, because the Arabs did not raid it as they raided the rest of the lands, and no one would violate its sanctity. ﴿And people are being snatched away from around them﴾ is an expression for what befalls people other than the people of Makkah of fighting or the seizure of their wealth.

The commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 29, verse 69:

﴿And those who strive for Us﴾. He means: the striving of the self (jihad al-nafs), which includes patience in enduring the harm of the disbelievers, bearing the leaving of one's homeland, and other such things. It has been said that it means fighting (qital), but this is weak, because fighting had not been commanded at the time this verse was revealed. ﴿We will surely guide them to Our paths﴾, that is, We will grant them success in the path of goodness. ﴿And indeed, Allah is with the doers of good﴾. The meaning is that He is with them through His help and His support.
